items.followUp: What happens to the temperature of a solution when dissolution is exothermic, and why?

rubric.why: Assesses how heat is released during dissolution.
rubric.description: Explains that forming attractions between solute and solvent particles releases heat.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking formation of solute–solvent attractions with heat release.

rubric.why: Assesses the condition for net heat release during dissolution.
rubric.description: States that more energy is released forming attractions than is absorbed separating particles, so the process is exothermic and the solution warms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the net energy condition or its effect on the solution temperature.

modelAnswer: When solute and solvent particles form attractions, energy is released as heat.
If the energy released is greater than the energy absorbed separating the particles, heat is given out overall and the solution temperature rises.

items.followUp: Give three differences between Rutherford’s and Bohr’s atomic theories.

rubric.why: Checks the difference in the permitted electron orbits.
rubric.description: Contrasts Rutherford’s unrestricted electron orbits with Bohr’s fixed, allowed orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct contrast about the orbits electrons may occupy.

rubric.why: Checks the theories’ treatment of radiation from orbiting electrons.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s model predicts radiation or energy loss, whereas electrons in Bohr’s stationary orbits do not radiate energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct contrast about radiation or energy loss.

rubric.why: Checks the consequence of the models for atomic stability.
rubric.description: Contrasts the instability implied by Rutherford’s model with the stability of Bohr’s model.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct contrast about atomic stability.

rubric.why: Checks the theories’ ability to explain the hydrogen line spectrum.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s theory cannot explain the hydrogen spectrum, whereas Bohr’s theory can.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct comparison about explaining the spectrum.

rubric.why: Checks Bohr’s explanation of spectral lines.
rubric.description: Explains that spectral lines arise when electrons absorb or emit definite energy while moving between allowed energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking electron transitions between energy levels with definite energy changes or spectral lines.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s theory allows electrons to revolve around the nucleus in any orbit; Bohr’s theory allows electrons only in fixed orbits.
In Rutherford’s model, orbiting electrons radiate energy; in Bohr’s model, electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate energy.
Rutherford’s model therefore implies that electrons lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, making the atom unstable; Bohr’s model accounts for stable atoms.
Rutherford’s theory cannot explain the hydrogen line spectrum, whereas Bohr’s theory explains it.
Bohr explained spectral lines by proposing that electrons absorb or emit definite energy when they jump between allowed energy levels.
